name: Coded Inequalities — Chaining Symbols to Find What's Certain
whatIsIt: Coded inequality questions replace >, <, =, ≥, ≤ with made-up symbols (like @, $, %, &, #), give you a legend explaining what each symbol means, then chain several coded statements together. You decode the chain into a single combined relationship and check which conclusions definitely follow.
whyNeeded: Once decoded, these questions are pure chain-comparison logic (just like statement-conclusion), but the disguise trips people up. Learning to decode calmly, then chain the real symbols, makes these some of the fastest-scoring questions once practiced.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking, and railway exams
Reading any notation-heavy technical document by first decoding the symbol legend
General comfort with symbolic/algebraic chains of relationships

vocabulary.meaning: The list at the start of the question defining what each made-up symbol means (e.g. '@ means greater than').
Combining two or more coded relations that share a middle term into one overall relation.

When the combined relation is uncertain between two possibilities (e.g. could be > or =), and those two possibilities exactly match two given conclusions — then neither conclusion follows alone, but 'either conclusion I or II follows' is true.

story.title: The Secret Symbol Code
story.text: Uncle Ben shows Ira a legend: '@ means greater than, % means greater than or equal to.' Then the statement: 'A @ B, B % C.' Ira first rewrites it in plain symbols: A > B, and B ≥ C. 'Now chain them,' says Uncle Ben. 'A is bigger than B, and B is at least as big as C — so no matter what, A must be bigger than C too.' Ira writes A > C confidently — the code was just a costume over ordinary logic.
story.extractedProblem: Legend: @ = greater than, % = greater than or equal to. Statement: A @ B, B % C. What is the definite relationship between A and C?
story.answerInStory: A > C, always — decode first, then chain exactly like a normal comparison.

visual.caption: Decode every coded symbol into a real >, <, =, ≥, or ≤ first, then chain them along a number-track exactly like an ordinary comparison ladder.

teachingGallery.title: Decode, then chain
teachingGallery.note: Never try to reason in the made-up symbols directly. Rewrite the whole statement in real >, <, = symbols first — then it's the same ladder-chaining you already know.

examples.caption: A > B ≥ C chains to A > C for certain. A ≥ B ≥ C only chains to A ≥ C — which could be > or =, so it's an 'either-or' case.

standardMethod.summary: Rewrite every coded symbol as its real meaning (>, <, =, ≥, ≤) using the legend. Chain relations that share a middle term into one combined relation. Compare each conclusion to the combined relation: if it matches exactly, it follows; if it's impossible, it doesn't; if the combined relation is uncertain between two options that exactly match two conclusions, it's an 'either-or' case.
steps: Write out the legend as plain symbols so you don't have to think in code.
Rewrite the full statement using only real >, <, =, ≥, ≤ symbols.
Chain together any relations sharing a common middle letter into one overall relation between the two end letters.
Check each conclusion against the combined relation: exact match = follows; impossible = doesn't follow.
If the combined relation is uncertain (e.g. ≥, which could be > or =) and the two conclusions exactly cover both possibilities, mark it as an either-or case.

alternateMethods.name: Strict-vs-loose chaining rule
alternateMethods.whenToUse: Any time you chain two relations together.
steps: If BOTH links are strict (> or <), the combined relation is strict.
If AT LEAST ONE link is strict and the other is ≥/≤ (loose) in the same direction, the combined relation is still strict.
If BOTH links are loose (≥ or ≤) in the same direction, the combined relation is loose (≥ or ≤) — an either-or case.
alternateMethods.example: A > B, B ≥ C → strict wins → A > C definitely. A ≥ B, B ≥ C → both loose → A ≥ C only (either > or =).

workedExamples.problem: Legend: @ = greater than (>), % = greater than or equal to (≥), # = equal to (=). Statement: A @ B, B % C. Conclusions: I. A @ C (A>C). II. A # C (A=C). Which follow?
steps: Decode: A @ B means A > B. B % C means B ≥ C.
Chain: A > B and B ≥ C — one link is strict (>), so the combined relation is strict: A > C, definitely.
Conclusion I says A > C — this matches exactly, so it follows.
Conclusion II says A = C — this contradicts the guaranteed A > C, so it does not follow.

workedExamples.problem: Legend: % = greater than or equal to (≥). Statement: P % Q, Q % R. Conclusions: I. P @ R meaning P > R. II. P # R meaning P = R. Which follow?
steps: Decode: P % Q means P ≥ Q. Q % R means Q ≥ R.
Chain: both links are loose (≥), so the combined relation is loose too: P ≥ R — which could be P > R OR P = R, we can't tell which.
Conclusion I (P > R) alone is not guaranteed — sometimes P could equal R. So I alone does not follow.
Conclusion II (P = R) alone is not guaranteed either — sometimes P could be strictly greater. So II alone does not follow.
But P ≥ R means one of the two MUST be true (it's either strictly greater, or exactly equal) — so 'either I or II follows' is the correct answer, even though neither follows alone.
workedExamples.answer: Neither follows alone, but either I or II follows

trickPractice.intro: Never reason in the made-up symbols. Convert to real >,<,=,≥,≤ before doing anything else.

questions.q: Legend: $ = less than (<). Statement: X $ Y. In plain symbols, what is X compared to Y?
A > B, B ≥ C — is the combined relation between A and C strict (>) or loose (≥, either-or)?
A ≥ B, B ≥ C — is the combined relation strict or an either-or case?

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to reason directly with the made-up symbols (@, $, %) instead of decoding them to real >, <, = first.
commonMistakes.fix: Always rewrite the whole statement in real symbols before doing any comparison — the made-up symbols are just a costume, not a new kind of logic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a chain with one strict (>) and one loose (≥) link as uncertain, when it's actually guaranteed strict.
commonMistakes.fix: Remember: strict beats loose. If even one link in the chain is strict, the whole combined relation is strict.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring 'neither conclusion follows' when two conclusions together exactly cover an either-or case, instead of recognizing that 'either I or II follows' is the correct answer.
commonMistakes.fix: When the combined relation is loose (≥ or ≤) and the two conclusions are exactly the strict and the equal version of it, check for the either-or pattern before giving up.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend the 'strict beats loose' chaining rule using A > B ≥ C (strict result) versus A ≥ B ≥ C (either-or result).

revisionCard.summary: Always decode coded symbols into real >, <, =, ≥, ≤ first using the legend. Chain relations sharing a middle term: if any link is strict, the combined result is strict; if all links are loose (≥ or ≤), the result is loose too — an either-or case between the strict and equal versions. Match each conclusion against the combined relation exactly.

gameMission.title: Crack the Symbol Code
gameMission.brief: Decode the jungle animals' secret comparison symbols and chain them to find out who's really bigger!

realLifeProject: Invent your own 3-symbol code for greater-than, less-than and equal-to, write two chained statements using it, and challenge a friend to decode and solve them.

rememberIt.unpack: Convert every made-up symbol to real >,<,=,≥,≤ before comparing anything.

studentQuestions.q: How do I remember 'strict beats loose'?
studentQuestions.a: Think of it like a relay race baton: as soon as one runner (link) proves a strict gap, that gap can never shrink back to equal — so the whole chain stays strict.

studentQuestions.q: Why does 'either-or' count as a valid answer?
studentQuestions.a: Because it's still a completely certain fact — you're 100% sure ONE of the two conclusions must be true, even without knowing which. That certainty is exactly what these questions test.
